title: He Survived Hiroshima. Then He Took the Train Home to Nagasaki
description:
Case 010, the full case file. Tsutomu Yamaguchi was born in Nagasaki in 1916 and worked as a draughtsman for Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, designing oil tankers. In 1945 the company sent him and two colleagues, Akira Iwanaga and Kuniyoshi Sato, to its shipyard in Hiroshima for about three months. On 6 August the job was done and the three were leaving for home when he realised he had left something behind and went back for it alone. At 8:15, walking toward the shipyard, he saw one aircraft and two small parachutes, and then the flash. He was about three kilometres from the centre of the explosion. His eardrums were ruptured, his upper body was burned and he was blinded for a time.

He found his two colleagues alive. The three spent the night in an air-raid shelter, and the next day made their way to a railway station and took a train to Nagasaki. His burns were treated and bandaged. On 9 August he reported for work at Mitsubishi anyway, and at about eleven o'clock he was describing Hiroshima to his supervisor, who did not believe that one bomb could destroy a city, when the second bomb exploded over Nagasaki. He was again about three kilometres away, and again he lived. His bandages were ruined and he was ill with a high fever for more than a week. His wife, Hisako, also lived through the Nagasaki bombing. The war ended on 15 August.

Afterwards he worked as a translator for the American occupation forces, then as a schoolteacher, and then returned to Mitsubishi to design tankers again. In 1957 he was registered as a survivor of the Nagasaki bombing only. For decades he said little in public. In his eighties he wrote a memoir and a book of poems. After his son died of cancer in 2005 he began to speak out: in 2006 he appeared in a documentary about people who were under both bombs (about 165 are thought to have been), which was shown at the United Nations in New York, where he asked for nuclear weapons to be abolished. In January 2009 he applied to have Hiroshima added to his record, and in March 2009 the Japanese government agreed, making him the only person it has officially recognised as a survivor of both bombings. He died of stomach cancer in Nagasaki on 4 January 2010, aged 93. Rook didn't believe it either.

The two bombings killed well over a hundred thousand people. This film follows one man's account and shows no victims; it is told with respect for all of them.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. His wife, his colleagues, the doctor, the officer, the clerk, the children and everyone else on screen are stand-ins, not likenesses of anyone, and every card, map, plan and record in the film is a drawing made for it, not a real document.
title_options: He Survived Hiroshima. Then He Took the Train Home to Nagasaki
The Man Who Lived Through Both Atomic Bombs: The Full Case of Tsutomu Yamaguchi
His Boss Didn't Believe One Bomb Could Destroy a City. Then the Windows Went White
Hiroshima on Monday, Nagasaki on Thursday, and He Lived to 93
Japan Has Recognised One Person as a Survivor of Both Bombs. This Is His Story
source_notes:
LONG-FORM RUN (14 Nov 2026). IMPORTANT LIMIT: this run's network policy blocked every source site (en.wikipedia.org, history.com, theweek.com, npr.org and the rest answered 'host not allowed'), so no page could be opened and read in full. What the run could do was search the web and read the search engine's summaries and quoted snippets of the pages listed under sources; each added fact below was accepted only when those snippets from at least two different sites agreed, or when the Short's run (which did open and read its seven sources, notes below unchanged) had already recorded it. Where only Wikipedia and pages that repeat it carry a detail, that is said. Nothing was taken from memory alone. Added facts and where each was found: born in Nagasaki in 1916 (Short's notes: 16 March 1916). A draughtsman who designed oil tankers for Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (Short's notes; Tokyo Weekender and Mental Floss snippets: 'Mitsubishi draftsmen', 'designing an oil tanker'). Sent to Hiroshima for about three months with two colleagues, Akira Iwanaga and Kuniyoshi Sato (Tokyo Weekender, Mental Floss, History.com snippets; Wikipedia per the Short's notes). The three were preparing to leave on 6 August (Wikipedia per the Short's notes; Tokyo Weekender; Biography.com says it was his last day there, The Week that he was due to leave the next day; the script says 'the job is done, and the three of them are leaving for home'). He went back for something he had forgotten: his hanko, a name seal (Wikipedia), or his travel permit or pass (Tokyo Weekender and one other snippet); the script says only 'something' and the shot shows him patting a pocket. Whether he was on a bus or on foot when he noticed differs; the film shows the three walking. 8:15, the aircraft and the two small parachutes, about 3 km, ruptured eardrums, burns to the upper body, temporary blindness: Short's notes. 'Half deaf' in the cold open rests on the ruptured eardrums; Wikipedia adds that he lost the hearing in his left ear for good. He found Iwanaga and Sato, who had also survived, and the three spent the night in an air-raid shelter (Mental Floss, History.com and Tokyo Weekender snippets; Short's notes). One snippet has him spending the night under an overturned boat instead; the film follows the majority account. The next day they made their way to a railway station and took a train to Nagasaki (History.com snippet: 'made their way toward the train station, which they had heard was somehow still operating'; Short's notes). One account says Yamaguchi and Iwanaga lost sight of Sato on the way though he was unhurt; the film keeps the three together on the platform and shows two colleagues in the carriage without saying who is who. Treated and bandaged in Nagasaki (Tokyo Weekender snippet: the Mitsubishi company hospital on 8 August; Wikipedia: received treatment); the film puts the doctor in a room at home, which is staging, and the narration says only 'his burns are treated'. Reported for work on 9 August, about 11 a.m., telling his supervisor, who did not believe one bomb could destroy a city; the white light; about 3 km again; thrown to the floor: Short's notes. Bandages ruined and a high fever with vomiting for over a week (Wikipedia; two other pages in the snippets say the same in their own words, probably after Wikipedia). His wife Hisako was also a survivor of the Nagasaki bombing (Wikipedia; several snippets); the film does not say where she was, and does not mention the black rain. Japan's surrender was announced on 15 August 1945, six days after Nagasaki (general history). Translator for the American occupation forces, then a schoolteacher, then back to Mitsubishi designing oil tankers (Wikipedia, Biography.com and two other snippets agree). 'He and Hisako raise a family': Wikipedia lists three children; the film shows three small figures and gives no names or dates, because the sources disagree about when the eldest was born. Registered in 1957 as a hibakusha of Nagasaki only (Wikipedia; History Net and Japan Times snippets). Said little in public for decades (Biography.com: 'shirked any public role until later in life'; Short's notes). A memoir and a book of poetry in his eighties (Wikipedia and its mirrors only). His son died of cancer in 2005 and after that he spoke out (two snippets; they give the son's age as 58 or 59, so the script gives none and does not name him). The 2006 documentary about double survivors, screened at the United Nations, where he asked for the abolition of nuclear weapons (Wikipedia and others; Short's notes); 'about a hundred and sixty-five' follows the NYT, The Week and Wikipedia, and the insert says it is an estimate and that counts differ. Applied in January 2009, accepted in March 2009, the only person officially recognised as a survivor of both (Wikipedia, Japan Times, NBC/AP, Short's notes). The remark in the 'said' segment is given as reported speech ('He is reported to have said that now the record could go on telling young people what happened, even after he was gone'): several outlets carry a version of it ('My double radiation exposure is now an official government record. It can tell the younger generation the horrifying history of the atomic bombings even after I die') but this run could not open the original Mainichi report, so it is not shown as a quotation. Died in Nagasaki on 4 January 2010, aged 93 (Short's notes). The last line, that he spent the time he had left asking that nobody ever be under a third, is Rook's summary of the campaigning described above, not a quotation. Left out on purpose: everything about the dead and injured around him (the film stays with one man and shows no victims); what he saw on the way to the station; the illnesses of his later life and of his wife and children; his son's name and age; his letter to President Obama and his meeting with James Cameron (not confirmed by this run's searches); the 2010 BBC QI controversy. Dramatised, not reported, in addition to the Short's list: the lodging street in Hiroshima, the dormitory and its gate (he was staying in company lodgings by some accounts; the building is invented); how his two colleagues looked and dressed; the farewell at his door and everything about his house and street in Nagasaki, including the brick office building, which carries no name; Hisako's looks and clothes, her being at his bedside, and the cloth and bowl; the room at home, the futon and the doctor; the railway carriage; the occupation office, the officer (no insignia, no flag) and the townsman; the classroom, the marks on the board and the pupils; the model tanker and the tanker plan (not a real ship); the three children at the table; his sitting on his step at dusk; the low table, brush and paper (the marks are plain strokes, not writing); the small shelf, the empty frame and the incense in the scene for his son's death, where no face is shown in the frame; the picture on the screen at the screening (a plain seated figure); the counter, the clerk, the booklet and the stamp (he was 93 and ill in 2009, and how the paperwork was actually done is not shown or claimed); his holding a booklet by the paper screens; the empty lectern; every card, clock, calendar and count (each is labelled an illustration, a sketch or drawn for the film); and everything Rook does. As in the Short, Rook is sceptical only before the flash; from then on he makes no jokes, and he leaves a paper crane instead of taking a keepsake. No dialogue is attributed to anyone.

SHORT'S NOTES (r010-yamaguchi): Read for this run (fetched 14 Nov 2026): Wikipedia (Tsutomu Yamaguchi); the New York Times obituary of 6 Jan 2010 as reprinted by History News Network; ABC News (6 Jan 2010); Justin McCurry's report of 25 Mar 2009 as carried by the Canberra Times; The Week's obituary (which quotes the Daily Telegraph and The Times); Biography.com; an NPR interview transcript (2010). The Guardian, NYT, BBC and History.com pages themselves could not be opened by this run. Agreed by the sources that mention each point: born in Nagasaki on 16 March 1916, so 29 in August 1945 (NYT: 'a 29-year-old engineer for Mitsubishi Heavy Industries'); a ship/oil-tanker designer; in Hiroshima on a business trip of about three months; ruptured eardrums, burns, temporary blindness; a night in an air-raid shelter (Wikipedia, NYT, McCurry); home to Nagasaki the following day (Wikipedia, NYT, McCurry, Biography.com), by train (McCurry: he 'stumbled to the train station the next day'; NPR); reported for work on 9 August still bandaged (Wikipedia, Biography.com, NPR, The Week); was telling his boss about Hiroshima when the second bomb exploded (NYT, Wikipedia, McCurry, The Week, Biography.com); the boss did not believe him (McCurry: 'reportedly questioned his sanity'; The Week quotes Yamaguchi's own account of the boss's words; Wikipedia); thrown to the floor but not seriously hurt the second time; died in Nagasaki on 4 January 2010 aged 93 of stomach cancer; recognised by the Japanese government in March 2009 as a survivor of both bombings and the only person officially recognised as one (ABC, NYT, McCurry, The Week, Wikipedia); spoke against nuclear weapons late in life, including at the United Nations in 2006 (NYT, The Week, Wikipedia, ABC). Where the sources differ: (1) Distance in Hiroshima: 'about 3 km (1.9 mi)' (Wikipedia) or 'less than 2 miles' (NYT, Biography.com) or 'two miles' (NPR); these agree, and the script says 'under two miles' while the sketch says 'about 3 km'. (2) What he was doing at 8:15: walking toward the docks after going back for his personal seal (Wikipedia), getting off a streetcar (NYT), or in or beside a field ditch (Biography.com and NPR, both from Charles Pellegrino's book). The film shows him walking a road toward the shipyard and claims no more; the fields beside the road are set dressing. Nothing in the film rests on Pellegrino's book alone: those details reach us only through that one book. (3) Whether 6 August was the last day of the trip (Biography.com; Wikipedia says he was 'preparing to leave the city') or the day before he was due to leave (The Week, from the Telegraph). The script says only that he 'is ending a work trip'. (4) Burns: 'left side of the top half of his body' (Wikipedia), 'upper torso' (NYT), 'face and arms' (The Week, Biography.com), 'covering his body' (ABC). The film shows bandages on his head, left arm and shoulder and says only 'burned'. (5) The time in Nagasaki: Wikipedia's Yamaguchi article says he was talking to his supervisor at 11:00 a.m.; the time on record for the explosion is 11:02 (Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum; nagasakipeace.jp), which is what the clock insert shows. (6) How many people were under both bombs: 'about 165' (NYT, The Week, Wikipedia body), 'at least 160' (Wikipedia lead), or nine identified by a 2005 study (ABC). All agree he is the only one officially recognised as a double survivor, so the script says 'Officially, the only one' and gives no count. (7) The Week says he was knocked unconscious the second time; Wikipedia says unhurt but ill with fever and vomiting for over a week; the film shows him thrown down and getting up and the narration says 'He lives again'. (8) When he began to speak publicly: 'in his eighties' he wrote a memoir (Wikipedia), 'not until 2005' (The Week), 'until the 2000s' (Biography.com). The script says 'those years' and the description says 'his last years'. Paraphrased from his own words, not quoted: 'the same white light fills the room' follows his remark to The Independent (reported by the NYT) that the same white light filled the room. No dialogue is attributed to anyone and the boss's words are not given. Left out on purpose: everything about the dead and injured around him (the film stays with one man and shows no victims), his wife and children (sources disagree about whether his son had been born by August 1945), the illnesses of his later life and of his family, the two colleagues who were with him in Hiroshima and also survived (Wikipedia names them; the shelter scene shows him alone), the 2010 BBC QI controversy, and his meeting with James Cameron. Shown but not narrated, from the sources: the single aircraft and the two small parachutes he described seeing (his own account, in The Week and Wikipedia), 8:15 (the time on record for Hiroshima), the train, the bandages, his being thrown to the floor in the office, 11:02, the lectern (he spoke at the United Nations in 2006 after a screening of a documentary about double survivors), the dates 6 and 9 August 1945, March 2009, the ages 29 and 93. Dramatised, not reported: what the road, shipyard, shelter, station, train, office and hall looked like (all generic; the station board is blank, the locomotive and aircraft carry no numbers or markings, the hall is not a model of any real room and its audience is plain silhouettes); how he, his boss and the two draughtsmen looked and dressed; the bag he carries; the exact way he fell and stood up both times; the lantern; the luggage; the personnel file and the 'survivor record' card (both labelled in the film as drawn for it; the real certificate is not reproduced); the two sketch maps (labelled as sketches, not to scale); the far cloud (a plain low-poly column, deliberately not detailed); and everything Rook does. Rook is sceptical only in the first seven seconds. From the flash onward he makes no jokes, takes his hat off, and at the end he leaves a folded paper crane on the platform bench instead of pocketing a keepsake, because this is not a case to take a souvenir from; the crane is a general symbol of remembrance in Japan and is not tied to Yamaguchi by any source.

quality_gate.method: Reviewed in four rounds with fixes after each. Round 1, the 16:9 3D contact sheet (69 stills): the man in the futon was hidden under the blanket, Rook stood inside the low table in the treatment scene and the wrapped arm was on the far side from the camera, Rook blocked the colleagues on the road and the clerk at the counter, the third man in the shelter was lost in the dark, the platform shot showed only backs, the fence hid the two figures on the step, a seated listener's head filled a corner of the empty-lectern shot, the microphone crossed the old man's face in the reused lectern angle, Rook was out of frame in the classroom; all restaged. Round 2, composited stills of all 85 shots with captions, HUD, inserts and overlays, plus the thumbnail: Rook was out of frame on the road again and half out of it in the classroom, the sign-off title sat on his head, and the thumbnail was rebuilt three times (a drawing table hid the man, then the camera was behind a wall). Round 3, a full-length low-resolution rehearsal (384x216, 4 samples, every 3D frame) composited at 1920x1080 with sound: it passed the automated gate locally (85 shots, mean 2.25 s, longest 4.02 s, loudness -15.3 LUFS, voice 15.2 dB over the bed, host in 36/85 shots (42%), closest match to an earlier episode 0.82). Round 4, frame strips of 24 shots from that rehearsal: the HUD fits (it only looked cut off in round 2 because stills are taken at the instant a HUD appears), the shipyard was showing while the farewell was being narrated so those two shots were swapped, the empty-lectern move was started further forward, the sign-off title moved right. After round 4 the storyboard was checked again by rule (85 shots, mean 2.25 s, no kind more than twice, none twice in a row, every kind defined, HOST lists every kind with Rook on screen) and the changed shots were spot-rendered, but the rehearsal was not rendered a second time. Audio was measured, not listened to. The fingerprint file the local gate wrote was deleted, not committed. The repository tests pass. The full-resolution render and the final gate run in the cloud.
